title: Key Concepts
description: The ideas that the rest of chemistry builds on, explained from scratch. Terms in other pages link here.

entries.name: Atoms and subatomic particles
entries.tagline: Everything is made of atoms, and every atom is built from three kinds of particle.

sections.text: An atom has a tiny, dense nucleus made of protons and neutrons. Electrons move around it in the space outside the nucleus.

facts: Charge +1, mass about 1 u, found in the nucleus.
No charge, mass about 1 u, found in the nucleus.
Charge −1, mass about 1/1836 u, found around the nucleus.

points: The number of protons decides which element the atom is.
In a neutral atom the number of electrons equals the number of protons.
Almost all the mass is in the nucleus, but almost all the volume is the electron cloud around it.

quiz.q: Which particle in an atom has a negative charge?

entries.name: Isotopes
entries.tagline: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.

sections.text: All atoms of an element have the same number of protons, but the number of neutrons can differ. Each version is called an isotope.

points: Carbon-12 has 6 protons and 6 neutrons. Carbon-14 has 6 protons and 8 neutrons.
The number after the name is the mass number: protons plus neutrons.
Isotopes of one element react almost identically, because chemistry depends on the electrons.
Some isotopes are unstable and radioactive. Carbon-14 is used to date ancient organic material.

quiz.q: Two isotopes of the same element differ in their number of…

entries.name: Valence electrons
entries.tagline: The outermost electrons of an atom, which decide how it bonds.

sections.text: Valence electrons are the electrons in the outermost occupied shell. Chemical reactions involve only these electrons.

points: For the main groups, the group number tells you how many: group 1 has 1, group 2 has 2. For groups 13 to 18 it is the group number minus 10, so group 17 has 7 and group 18 has 8 (helium has 2).
Atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons to reach a full outer shell, usually 8. This is the octet rule.
This is why elements in the same group react in similar ways.

quiz.q: How many valence electrons does a halogen (group 17) have?

entries.name: Electron shells and orbitals
entries.tagline: How the electrons are arranged around the nucleus.

sections.text: Electrons sit in shells numbered 1, 2, 3 and so on, counting out from the nucleus. Each shell is divided into subshells named s, p, d and f. Each subshell is made of orbitals, which are regions where an electron is likely to be found.

points: Each orbital holds at most two electrons.
Orbitals fill from the lowest energy to the highest. This is called the Aufbau principle.
Shell 1 has only s. Shell 2 has s and p. Shell 3 has s, p and d. Shell 4 adds f.
An electron configuration is a list of which subshells are filled, such as 1s² 2s² 2p⁶.

quiz.q: How many electrons can a p subshell hold?

entries.name: Radioactivity
entries.tagline: Unstable nuclei that give off radiation as they change.

sections.text: Some nuclei are unstable. They change into other nuclei by releasing particles or energy, a process called radioactive decay. Technetium (43), promethium (61) and every element heavier than lead have no truly stable isotope.

points: The half-life is the time for half of a sample's nuclei to decay. It ranges from fractions of a second to billions of years.
Alpha decay releases a helium nucleus, beta decay releases an electron or positron, and gamma radiation is high-energy light.
Uses include medical imaging, cancer treatment, dating old objects and nuclear power.

quiz.q: What is a half-life?
quiz.a: The time for half of a radioactive sample to decay
wrong: Half the time an element takes to melt
The time for an atom to lose half its electrons
Half of the age of an atom

entries.name: Phase changes and sublimation
entries.tagline: How matter moves between solid, liquid and gas.

sections.text: Matter exists mainly as a solid, a liquid or a gas. Moving from one to another is a phase change, and each change has its own name.

facts: Solid straight to gas, with no liquid stage.

points: Melting and boiling points depend on pressure. Tables give them at normal atmospheric pressure, 1 atm.
Dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) sublimes at everyday pressure. Iodine and arsenic also sublime.

quiz.q: What is it called when a solid turns directly into a gas?

entries.name: Kelvin and temperature
entries.tagline: The temperature scale that starts at the coldest possible temperature.

sections.text: The kelvin (K) is the SI unit of temperature. Zero kelvin is absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature, where particles have the least possible energy.

points: A change of one kelvin is the same size as a change of one degree Celsius.
Water freezes at 273.15 K and boils at 373.15 K at 1 atm.
Kelvin values are never negative, which makes them convenient for gas and energy calculations.

quiz.q: What is 0 K in degrees Celsius?

entries.name: Ions
entries.tagline: Atoms or molecules that carry an electric charge.

sections.text: An atom becomes an ion by gaining or losing electrons. Losing electrons gives a positive ion, called a cation. Gaining electrons gives a negative ion, called an anion.

points: Metals tend to lose electrons. Sodium becomes Na⁺ and calcium becomes Ca²⁺.
Nonmetals tend to gain electrons. Chlorine becomes Cl⁻ and oxygen becomes O²⁻.
The charge is the number of electrons lost or gained, written as a superscript with + or −.
Ions with opposite charges attract each other and form ionic compounds.

quiz.q: What is a positively charged ion called?

entries.name: Ionic and covalent bonds
entries.tagline: The two main ways atoms are held together.

sections.text: In an ionic bond, one atom hands electrons to another, and the oppositely charged ions attract. In a covalent bond, atoms share pairs of electrons.

facts: Usually a metal with a nonmetal, such as NaCl. Solid at room temperature with a high melting point. Conducts electricity when molten or dissolved.
Usually nonmetals only, such as H₂O or CO₂. Can be a gas, liquid or solid. Small molecules have low melting points.

points: A salt is an ionic compound. Table salt is sodium chloride, NaCl.
The difference in electronegativity predicts the bond: a large difference gives an ionic bond and a small one gives a covalent bond.

quiz.q: In a covalent bond, the atoms…

entries.name: Chemical equations and balancing
entries.tagline: A reaction written in symbols, with the same atoms on both sides.

sections.text: Reactants are written on the left of the arrow and products on the right. Atoms are never created or destroyed in a reaction. This is conservation of mass, so each element must appear the same number of times on both sides.
There are 4 hydrogen atoms and 2 oxygen atoms on each side.

points: Balance by changing the numbers in front of formulas, called coefficients. Never change the small subscripts inside a formula, because that changes the substance.
State symbols can be added: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas and (aq) dissolved in water.
A double arrow ⇌ means the reaction is reversible.

quiz.q: When balancing an equation, you may change…
quiz.a: The coefficients in front of formulas

entries.name: Exothermic and endothermic reactions
entries.tagline: Whether a reaction gives out heat or takes it in.

sections.text: In an exothermic reaction, energy is released to the surroundings, usually as heat, so things get warmer. In an endothermic reaction, energy is absorbed, so things get colder.

facts: Burning fuel, neutralization, rusting. The enthalpy change ΔH is negative.
Heating limestone to make lime, photosynthesis, a cold pack dissolving ammonium nitrate. ΔH is positive.

points: ΔH is the heat change at constant pressure, usually in kJ per mole.
Breaking bonds takes energy and making bonds releases it. The balance decides which kind of reaction it is.

quiz.q: A reaction that releases heat to its surroundings is…

entries.name: Catalysts
entries.tagline: A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up.

sections.text: A catalyst gives the reaction an easier route with a lower activation energy, which is the energy barrier the reactants must get over.

points: It is not consumed, so a small amount can be used again and again.
It does not change how much product there is at equilibrium. It only changes how fast equilibrium is reached.
Examples: iron in making ammonia, platinum in car exhaust converters, and enzymes, the catalysts in living cells.

quiz.q: What does a catalyst do?
quiz.a: Speeds up a reaction without being used up
wrong: Makes the reaction release more heat
Is consumed as the reaction runs

entries.name: Chemical equilibrium
entries.tagline: When a reversible reaction settles into a steady balance.

sections.text: Some reactions can run in both directions. At equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions go at the same rate, so the amounts of reactants and products stop changing, even though both reactions are still happening.
If you disturb a system at equilibrium, it shifts to oppose the change.
points: Adding reactant or removing product pushes the equilibrium toward the products.
Raising the pressure favors the side with fewer gas molecules.
Raising the temperature favors the endothermic direction, and lowering it favors the exothermic direction.

quiz.q: At chemical equilibrium…
quiz.a: The forward and reverse reaction rates are equal
wrong: All the reactants are used up
The amounts of reactants and products are equal

entries.name: Precipitates and solubility
entries.tagline: A solid that appears when two clear solutions are mixed.

sections.text: A precipitate is an insoluble solid that forms in a solution. It appears when ions from the two solutions combine into a compound that does not dissolve in water.
Silver chloride is a white solid.

sections.h: Rules of thumb for what dissolves
points: All nitrates, and salts of sodium and potassium, dissolve.
Most chlorides dissolve. Silver chloride does not, and lead(II) chloride is only slightly soluble.
Most sulfates dissolve. Barium sulfate and lead(II) sulfate do not.
Most hydroxides and carbonates do not dissolve, except those of group 1.

quiz.q: What is a precipitate?
quiz.a: An insoluble solid that forms in a solution
wrong: A gas given off in a reaction
A liquid layer that floats on top

entries.name: Acids and bases
entries.tagline: Substances that give away or take up hydrogen ions.

sections.text: In the Brønsted–Lowry definition, an acid donates a hydrogen ion (H⁺) and a base accepts one. A base that dissolves in water is called an alkali, and it releases hydroxide ions (OH⁻).

points: Below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral and above 7 is basic, at 25 °C.
Each step on the scale is a tenfold change in the concentration of hydrogen ions.

facts: Hydrochloric acid (HCl), sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄), nitric acid (HNO₃), and acetic acid in vinegar.
Sodium hydroxide (NaOH), calcium hydroxide, and ammonia (NH₃).

sections.text: An acid and a base react together to give a salt and water.

quiz.q: What is the pH of a neutral solution at 25 °C?

entries.name: Hydrocarbons and fuels
entries.tagline: Compounds made only of carbon and hydrogen, the main fuels we burn.

sections.text: Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen. They are the main parts of natural gas, petrol (gasoline) and diesel, and they release a lot of energy when they burn.
These are alkanes. They have only single bonds and follow the formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.

quiz.q: Which two elements make up a hydrocarbon?

entries.name: Oxidation states
entries.tagline: A bookkeeping number that tracks where the electrons are.

sections.text: The oxidation state, or oxidation number, is the charge an atom would have if all its bonds were treated as fully ionic. It is a tool for following electrons through a reaction.

points: An atom in a pure element is 0: Na, O₂ and Cl₂ are all 0.
A simple ion equals its charge: Na⁺ is +1 and Cl⁻ is −1.
Oxygen is usually −2. Hydrogen is usually +1 when bonded to nonmetals.
In a neutral compound the oxidation states add up to 0. In an ion they add up to the charge of the ion.
H₂O: hydrogen is +1 (twice) and oxygen is −2, which adds up to 0.
CO₂: oxygen is −2 (twice), so carbon must be +4.

sections.text: If an atom's oxidation state goes up, it has been oxidized. If it goes down, it has been reduced.

quiz.q: What is the oxidation state of oxygen in O₂?
What is the oxidation state of carbon in CO₂?

entries.name: Oxidation and reduction
entries.tagline: Losing and gaining electrons, which always happen together.

sections.text: Oxidation is the loss of electrons. Reduction is the gain of electrons. One cannot happen without the other, so the pair is called a redox reaction.
Sodium goes from 0 to +1, so it is oxidized. Chlorine goes from 0 to −1, so it is reduced.

points: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain, of electrons.
The oxidizing agent takes the electrons, so it is the one that gets reduced. The reducing agent gives the electrons, so it is the one that gets oxidized.
Oxidation does not need oxygen. Oxygen is just a very common oxidizing agent, which is where the name comes from.

quiz.q: In a redox reaction, the species that loses electrons is…

entries.name: The activity series
entries.tagline: A ranking of metals by how easily they lose electrons.

sections.text: The activity series lists metals, and hydrogen, from most reactive to least reactive. A more reactive metal loses electrons more easily.
Potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, lead, (hydrogen), copper, silver, gold.

points: A metal can replace any metal below it in the series, but not one above it. Zinc can replace copper in copper sulfate, but copper cannot replace zinc.
Metals above hydrogen react with acids to give hydrogen gas. Metals below it do not.
Very reactive metals such as potassium and sodium react even with cold water.

quiz.q: Which metal can displace copper from copper sulfate solution?

entries.name: Electrolysis
entries.tagline: Using electricity to force a reaction to happen.

sections.text: Electrolysis uses an electric current to drive a reaction that would not happen by itself. The current passes through a molten or dissolved ionic compound called the electrolyte.

points: At the negative electrode (the cathode), positive ions gain electrons. That is reduction.
At the positive electrode (the anode), negative ions lose electrons. That is oxidation.
A memory aid: RED CAT, AN OX. Reduction at the cathode, oxidation at the anode.

sections.text: Electrolysis is used to make aluminium, chlorine and sodium hydroxide, and to electroplate metals.

quiz.q: At which electrode does reduction happen in electrolysis?
